Sounds good. I have another observation that I want to add to research and this is my own, but it is something that I want to be part of the frameworks.

I don't know which chapter this would go into but I think that one of the best rules for intimacy I have seen is that you explain to your partner that you have needs, they have needs, and that we love each other and we want to serve those needs.

Sex is an important part of many people's need profile, particularly men. It is less important for women, often for a variety of reasons, including some of it being medical or health-related. I like what I've seen some couples agree to, which is that, at the end of the day, you set a time period: you go no longer than that before you have sex. Some people do it once a week, some people say every 3 days.

The other addendum to that rule is that if one person initiates and the other person says no, then that person who said no has 24 hours to reinitiate with the person. What that means is sometimes you don't feel like it and that's okay but you do need to put in the work to basically express love in one of the many ways, with physicality being one of those.

Second, the rules of engagement make it fair so that nobody feels rejected. People should be able to say no anytime they want to. It's their body, their right but on the flip side, constant rejection leads to resentment and bitterness. By putting it on the person who rejected to then initiate, that removes the rejection.

The last part is that sometimes it's okay. I like, in the framework, when the person initiates and the other person doesn't really feel like it, it needs to be something where the person who doesn't feel like it can also say, "Hey I'm going to need you to really put in the work to make me an enthusiastic participant." What is good about this is that the person is willing to do it. It just might not feel very sexy at the moment and so it's asking the initiator to raise the bar to make sure that it is romantic and enjoyable, etc.

These three rules are quite good:
- Set frequency.
- The ability to communicate that you're not into it.
- The bar gets raised by the initiator.


Rejection then puts the IOU on the other person and all of this is built on a foundation of "we have needs and we serve each other and love each other."
